scenarios.title: The Franchise Legend
scenarios.text: The first club that ever signed you wants to recognize what you gave it: a night in your name, a banner, and the old equipment manager, retired now, asking to present you with your first helmet.

choices.label: Accept the helmet
choices.result: The old helmet, handed over by the old equipment manager at midfield, scuffed and too small. You both hold it up, and the crowd remembers you as a rookie.

choices.label: Ask them to honor the staff
choices.result: A request that the night honor the staff from your rookie year too: the trainers, the cooks, the laundry crew. The club agrees, and the photo has forty people in it.

choices.label: Make it a family night
choices.result: Your family on the field with you, {sibling} wearing your rookie jersey. It's loud and happy, and {sibling} does a victory dance that the cameras love.

choices.label: Tell the story of the rookie check
choices.result: The truth, told into the microphone: you spent your whole rookie check in a month, and this club's staff helped you grow up. The crowd laughs, and the old equipment manager cries.
choices.lock_text: having spent your rookie check fast

scenarios.title: The Jersey Retirement Discussion
scenarios.text: A club is discussing retiring your number once you're done. The general manager wants to know how you'd feel about it, and whether there's a young player you'd rather see wear it.

choices.label: Retire it
choices.result: Retire it, you say, honored and a little embarrassed. The club plans a ceremony for whenever you stop, and the number goes on a list nobody can touch.

choices.label: Give it to a young player
choices.result: Give it to a young player, you say, and name one. The kid hears about it and can't speak for a full minute, and promises to wear it properly.

choices.label: Let the fans decide
choices.result: Let the fans decide, you suggest. The vote runs for a month, the comments are wonderful, and the result surprises everyone, including the general manager.

scenarios.title: The All-Time Record
scenarios.text: You could become the league's career scoring leader this season, and the league office calls to ask how you'd want the moment marked, if it comes: a ceremony, a pause, or nothing at all.

choices.label: Ask for nothing
choices.result: Nothing at all, you tell them: no pause, no ceremony, just the next play. The league is surprised and agrees, and the specialists say it's the most you thing you've ever done.

choices.label: Ask for the old kickers
choices.result: If it comes, you'd like the living kickers who held the record before you to be there. The league calls them all, and every one of them says yes.

choices.label: Ask for your family
choices.result: Your family on the sideline, if it comes, and nothing else. The league arranges passes, and {parent} starts planning an outfit that very evening.

scenarios.title: The Longevity Record
scenarios.text: You're close to the record for most seasons by a kicker, and a historian calls to interview you for a book about long careers. She has a list of every kicker who lasted, and the reasons each one stopped.

choices.label: Read her list
choices.result: Her whole list, read carefully, every reason every kicker stopped. It's sobering and kind, and it makes you grateful for every morning your leg still works.

choices.label: Give her the whole story
choices.result: Hours of interviews, every slump, every injury, every year you thought was the last. Her chapter about you is the longest in the book, and the most honest.

choices.label: Keep the interview short
choices.result: A short interview, and back to practice. The record isn't something you want to think about until it's behind you, if it ever is.

scenarios.title: The Documentary Premiere
scenarios.text: The documentary about your career premieres at a small theater downtown: a red carpet the length of a hallway, your old coaches in the third row, and a director who keeps squeezing your arm.

choices.label: Watch it with the audience
choices.result: You sit in the audience and watch your whole life on a big screen. The parts you'd forgotten hit hardest, and you need a minute in the lobby afterwards.

choices.label: Skip it and watch at home
choices.result: At home instead, later, alone with the dog. It's easier that way, and you text the director a long message at two in the morning.

choices.label: Bring the whole unit
choices.result: The snapper and {holder}, brought as your guests, in suits they complain about all night. They cheer for every kick on screen like it's live, and the audience joins in.

scenarios.title: A Night in the Hall
scenarios.text: A quarterback you played with is inducted into the Hall of Fame, and he's asked you to introduce him. The speech has a time limit, and he has already told you not to mention the time with the goat.

choices.label: Mention the goat
choices.result: The goat, mentioned, within the time limit. The audience roars, he covers his face, and his speech afterwards starts with 'Thanks for nothing.'

choices.label: Keep it serious
choices.result: A serious introduction, about what he was like on the hard days nobody saw. He's in tears by the end, and so is half the room.

choices.label: Let his family tell it
choices.result: Half your time given to his children, who tell the story better than you could. It's the best introduction of the night, and he hugs you for a long time.

scenarios.title: The Hall of Fame Dinner
scenarios.text: You're invited to a dinner for the league's greats, a long table in a private room, and you're the only one still playing. The others keep asking how your knees are, with genuine concern.

choices.label: Listen more than you talk
choices.result: You listen far more than you talk, all night, to stories you'll never hear anywhere else. Driving home, you realize you've been given a map of what comes next.

choices.label: Ask about stopping
choices.result: A question for the table: how did each of them know it was time? The answers go around the room, honest and funny, and the dinner runs two hours late.

choices.label: Talk about the young players
choices.result: You talk about the young players you've seen this year, and the legends lean in. Two of them ask for names, and a week later one of them visits your club's camp.

scenarios.title: The Final Road Game
scenarios.text: Your family comes along for what could be your last road trip: a hotel floor of relatives, a bus to the stadium, and {parent} wearing a jersey with your name spelled the old way.

choices.label: Spend the evening with them
choices.result: An evening with the family at the hotel, room service and stories, home to your own room by ten. They talk about it for years.

choices.label: Keep your routine
choices.result: Your routine, kept exactly, with a family breakfast the morning after the game. They understand completely, and the breakfast runs until checkout.

choices.label: Give them the stadium tour
choices.result: A tour of the stadium the afternoon before, arranged with the home team's staff. {sibling} runs out of the tunnel like a player, and nobody stops them.

scenarios.title: The Team's Tribute Video
scenarios.text: Your teammates and coaches have put together a tribute video, and they want to show it at the team meeting tomorrow. {holder} has warned you, quietly, to bring tissues and to sit near the door.

choices.label: Watch it with everyone
choices.result: You watch it with the whole team, in the meeting room, with the lights off. When it ends nobody turns the lights on for a while, and that's how you know it worked.

choices.label: Make a joke first
choices.result: A joke before it starts, to take the pressure off, and the room laughs. Then the video plays, and the joke doesn't help at all.

choices.label: Thank {holder} for the warning
choices.result: Over coffee before the meeting, {holder} gets thanked for the warning. They admit they made half the video, and you sit near the door, as told.

scenarios.title: The New Generation
scenarios.text: A young kicker on another club asks you to be his mentor: a phone call a week, film by email, and the honesty nobody on his own staff gives him. He apologizes twice for asking.

choices.label: Say yes
choices.result: Yes, and you mean it: a call every Sunday night, film every Monday, honesty always. He gets better quickly, and so does your own eye for kicking.

choices.label: Say yes, with conditions
choices.result: Yes, with conditions: he tells his own coaches, and he does the work before he calls. He agrees, and the conditions make the whole thing better.

choices.label: Point him somewhere better
choices.result: A kind no, and the name of a coach who'd be better for him than you right now. He's disappointed, then grateful, and the coach turns out perfect.

scenarios.title: The Coaching Job
scenarios.text: A club offers you a coaching job, starting the day you retire: special teams coordinator, a staff of three, and an office with a window over the practice field.

choices.label: Accept for later
choices.result: Accepted, for whenever you're ready. Knowing the window is waiting makes the present lighter, and you start keeping a notebook of drills.

choices.label: Ask for a trial
choices.result: A trial, on your bye week, running one practice. You love it and you're bad at the whistle, and the players say you'll be great.

choices.label: Say coaching isn't for you
choices.result: Coaching isn't for you, you decide, after a long walk. You'd rather teach kids than run a staff, and the club respects the honesty.

scenarios.title: The Analyst Offer
scenarios.text: A network wants you as its lead football analyst once you retire: the big games, the studio, and a wardrobe person who has already asked for your measurements.

choices.label: Sign for later
choices.result: Signed for later, with a start date that reads 'when ready'. The wardrobe person sends a swatch book, and you laugh at every page.

choices.label: Ask to try a broadcast
choices.result: One broadcast first, on a bye week, beside a veteran announcer. You're nervous and good, and the network calls the next morning with a better offer.

choices.label: Stay on the field
choices.result: No, with thanks: you'd rather be on a field than talking about one. The network says the door stays open, and you believe them.

choices.label: Bring your old producer
choices.result: You agree on one condition: your old radio producer comes too. The network agrees, and the two of you start planning segments over the phone like nothing ever ended.
choices.lock_text: having hosted your own radio show

scenarios.title: The Front Office
scenarios.text: A club discusses a front-office job with you: scouting, contracts, the business side you've watched from the locker room for years. The general manager says you'd see the game from the other side of the desk.

choices.label: Learn the business now
choices.result: A few hours a week with the front office now, learning contracts and scouting. It's fascinating and humbling, and your own negotiations will never be the same.

choices.label: Ask about the hard parts
choices.result: The hard parts, asked about directly: cutting players, saying no, telling a rookie it's over. The answers are honest, and they make you think for a long time.

choices.label: Decline for now
choices.result: Not now: you still have a leg and a job on the field. The general manager shakes your hand and says the desk will wait.

choices.label: Ask about the integrity work
choices.result: You ask about the integrity side, the part you once saw up close when you reported a bookie. The general manager offers you that role specifically, and it fits.
choices.lock_text: having reported a bookie to the league
